name: Mastra
description: TypeScript framework for AI applications and agents
scored_configuration: @mastra/core Agent and Mastra instance with default constructor arguments; first-class features (Workspace with LocalFilesystem/LocalSandbox, Memory, MCPClient, bundled server) scored at their own defaults.
headline: Mastra has a well-built human-approval gate and opt-in sandboxing, but almost none of it is on by default. Tools run without approval, the default LocalSandbox executes shell commands directly on the host, and nothing limits what an agent hijacked through a tool result can do. Deployers should enable requireToolApproval, use bubblewrap/Seatbelt or a remote sandbox, configure server auth, and add timeouts before exposing an agent to untrusted content.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: Mastra has no agent identity of its own: tools run inside the developer's Node process and use whatever credentials that process holds, with no per-tool or per-request credential scoping. Two good narrowing measures exist: the local command sandbox and MCP stdio servers get a scrubbed environment rather than the full process environment. The bundled HTTP server relies on the developer configuring authentication, and its default access control is not locked down. A hijacked agent can do whatever the developer's integration credentials allow.

S.finding: Tools execute in-process with the host's ambient credentials; the framework issues no scoped or per-tool identity.
S.gap: No dedicated, role-scoped identity for the agent or its tools.

evidence.note: no credential-narrowing primitive in the tool or agent layers

C.finding: Subprocess paths narrow ambient authority (LocalSandbox passes only PATH plus configured env; MCP stdio gets the SDK's curated env), but in-process tools see the full process environment and no authorization layer sits in the tool executor.
C.gap: No authorization layer that every tool path (including in-process tools and sub-agents) passes through.

D.finding: Server authentication is not configured by default, and the default access-control behaviour is not locked down.
D.gap: No authenticated, least-privilege default; per-user scoping requires the developer to configure server auth and mapUserToResourceId.

B.finding: A hijacked agent holds every credential the developer wired into the process and its tools; the framework adds no boundary beyond the subprocess env scrub.
B.gap: Credentials are long-lived and as broad as the developer configures; nothing narrows them to one system or tenant.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: Mastra has a well-built human approval mechanism: when enabled, a tool call suspends, the exact tool name and arguments are streamed to the client, and only a decision delivered through the workflow resume boundary (not model-written data) can approve or decline it. But it is off by default: every tool's requireApproval defaults to false, the agent-wide requireToolApproval is unset, and the workspace's file-write, delete and shell tools ship with approval disabled. Nothing in the framework provides undo for actions a tool takes.

cap.reason: The approval gate exists but tools default to requireApproval false and requireToolApproval is unset.

S.finding: Per-call approval suspends the run and shows the exact tool name and arguments; approval comes only from the workflow resume data, and policy functions that throw fail to 'requires approval'.
S.gap: No argument-level allow/deny/escalate policy layer shipped by the framework; policies are developer-written functions.

evidence.contains: resumeData is untrusted and cannot grant or decline consent

C.finding: When the global flag is set every registered tool (including MCP tools) passes the verdict, but a per-tool needsApprovalFn overrides the global seed, and unknown tools are not rejected.
C.gap: A per-tool or MCP server-level approval function can exempt calls that a global requireToolApproval: true meant to gate; no default-deny for unknown tools.

D.finding: Approval is opt-in: tools default to requireApproval false and workspace tools default to no approval.
D.gap: Approval is not on by default for consequential tools.

B.finding: Registered tools (and the workspace delete/write/shell tools) can take irreversible actions with no framework-level undo, preview or rate limit.
B.gap: No checkpoint/rollback or dry-run for the common case.

evidence.note: no checkpoint/rollback in the tool or agent layers

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Every Mastra tool built with createTool gets its input validated against its schema before it runs, and MCP tool schemas are converted so they are validated too; tools that arrive with a plain JSON schema (e.g. Vercel AI SDK tools) skip validation. The workspace filesystem tools are well scoped: paths are confined to the workspace by default with symlink-aware realpath checks. But the workspace also ships a free-form shell tool whose command string goes to the host shell, and all workspace tools are enabled by default once a workspace is attached.

S.finding: Typed schema validation for every standard-schema tool, plus realpath containment in LocalFilesystem; the execute_command tool accepts an arbitrary shell string.
S.gap: General tools are not replaced by narrow ones; the shell tool is raw passthrough and no URL/host allowlists apply to tools.

C.finding: createTool and MCP tools go through the shared validator, but tools with non-standard (plain JSON) schemas bypass it.
C.gap: Validation is not applied to every tool type through one central policy layer.

D.finding: A bare Agent has no tools, but attaching a Workspace enables all its tools, including write, delete and shell, by default; each can be disabled individually.
D.gap: Write/exec workspace tools are not off by default; no read-only default tool group.

B.finding: With the default LocalSandbox, the shell tool runs any command on the host as the developer's OS user, including in an absolute cwd outside the workspace.
B.gap: Misused tools are not limited to the workspace or bounded in quantity.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Agents only execute code if the developer attaches a Workspace with a sandbox, but the default sandbox, LocalSandbox, runs commands directly on the host through the system shell with isolation set to 'none'. Its environment is scrubbed to PATH plus configured variables, but the process still reaches the whole filesystem, the network, and anything else the OS user can. Opt-in isolation is solid: bubblewrap or Seatbelt confine writes to the workspace, deny network by default, and refuse to start if the backend is missing; remote sandboxes (E2B, Daytona, Modal and others) are also available. Because those are opt-in, the criterion is capped.

cap.reason: Opt-in mechanism: off in the scored default configuration.

S.finding: bwrap creates PID/IPC/UTS namespaces, unshares the network unless allowed, mounts system paths read-only and binds only the workspace read-write.
S.gap: Not kernel-separated (microVM/gVisor); no seccomp filter or resource limits in the profile.

C.finding: Foreground and background commands are wrapped by the isolation backend, and construction fails if the backend is unavailable rather than falling back to the host.
C.gap: MCP stdio servers and other extension processes are not sandboxed.

D.finding: The backend must be chosen explicitly; the default is 'none'.
D.gap: Isolation is not on by default.

B.finding: Workspace mounted read-write, network off by default, scrubbed env; but no CPU/memory/PID limits and the workspace persists.
B.gap: No CPU/memory/PID limits in the sandbox profile.

cap.reason: Sandboxing (bwrap/Seatbelt or a remote provider) exists but LocalSandbox defaults to isolation 'none'.

S.finding: LocalSandbox defaults to isolation 'none' and spawns commands with the host shell as the current user.
S.gap: No OS-level separation by default.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Nothing in the framework structurally limits what a hijacked agent can do. Tool results, MCP results and fetched content enter the conversation the same way as any other message, and no taint tracking or Rule-of-Two enforcement disables egress or writes once untrusted content has been read. Mastra ships an optional LLM-based PromptInjectionDetector, but it only checks the incoming user messages, not tool results, and it is a classifier rather than a boundary. Because approval is off by default, an injected instruction can both leak data and take irreversible actions with no human in the loop.

S.finding: An LLM classifier that can block/warn/rewrite detected injections.
S.gap: Detection only; no capability is removed once untrusted content is read.

C.finding: Runs as an input processor on incoming messages only; tool results are not scanned.
C.gap: Tool results, MCP outputs and sub-agent messages are not covered.

D.finding: Must be added explicitly as a processor.
D.gap: Not on by default.

B.finding: Same worst case as the default: leak plus irreversible action unattended.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Memory is opt-in per agent; the default Memory configuration persists the last 10 messages of each thread and replays them in later turns, with working memory and semantic recall off. Threads are tied to a resource (user) and the agent refuses to use a thread owned by a different resource. Nothing validates what is written: when working memory is enabled the model rewrites a free-text profile that is re-injected on every turn across all of that user's threads. Memory isolation is not a strict boundary.

S.finding: Persisted messages keep their roles, but writes are not validated; working memory (when enabled) is free text written by the model via a tool and re-injected.
S.gap: No provenance-as-data presentation or gating of memory writes.

C.finding: No memory path is validated or gated.
C.gap: Neither history, working memory nor semantic recall is controlled.

evidence.note: no validation on what flows into persisted history

D.finding: Threads and working memory are namespaced per thread/resource and ownership is enforced, but namespace isolation is not a strict boundary.
D.gap: Namespace isolation is not fully enforced.

B.finding: Poisoned history persists in the thread across sessions and can trigger tool use in later turns; resource-scoped working memory extends that across the user's threads.
B.gap: Poisoned memory is not limited to text output or gated actions.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: Mastra loads third-party code mainly as MCP servers that the developer lists in code: stdio servers are launched from whatever command is given (often an unpinned npx package) with no version pinning, hash check, or re-approval when tool definitions change. Stdio servers receive only the MCP SDK's curated environment plus explicitly configured variables, not the full process environment. Nothing is enabled automatically. Access control on the optional editor's stored MCP configs is not locked down.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: Model and integration API keys come from environment variables and stay in the developer's process; Mastra keeps them out of subprocesses by scrubbing the LocalSandbox and MCP stdio environments. When observability is enabled, a SensitiveDataFilter that redacts fields like password, token and apiKey is applied by default to traces. Plain logs are not redacted. Anonymous usage telemetry (token counts and feature use, no prompt content) is sent to PostHog by default unless MASTRA_TELEMETRY_DISABLED is set.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Out of the box, Mastra installs a no-op observability layer and logs tool execution only at debug level, which the default logger does not print, so there is no record of what an agent did unless the developer configures it. With observability enabled, every tool and MCP tool call becomes a structured span with arguments, run, thread and resource IDs, nested under the agent run, and can be exported to OpenTelemetry and other backends. Approvals and declines are not recorded as their own events, and exports are best-effort.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: Every agent run stops after 5 model steps unless the developer sets maxSteps or a stop condition. There is no default wall-clock or token/cost limit: run and step timeouts exist but are opt-in, and the local sandbox applies a command timeout only when one is passed (its documented 30-second default is not implemented in the process manager). When delegating, the model can raise a sub-agent's step budget if that sub-agent has no configured default, and each sub-agent starts its own budget. Abort signals are passed to tools and background shell processes can be killed by process group.

critical_findings.summary: The default LocalSandbox executes model-chosen shell commands directly on the host as the developer's OS user, with isolation 'none'.

evidence.contains: No sandboxing (direct execution on host) - default

critical_findings.summary: A hijacked agent can both leak data and take irreversible actions through any registered tool with no human involved, because approval is off by default and nothing tracks untrusted content.

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: Tool and MCP results enter context with no taint tracking (packages/core/src/processors/processors/prompt-injection-detector.ts:180 scans user input only)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Developer credentials in the process environment; per-user memory (packages/core/src/memory/memory.ts:90)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: Any registered tool without approval (packages/core/src/tools/tool.ts:384); workspace write/shell tools (packages/core/src/workspace/tools/tools.ts:152-153)

fixes.summary: Default requireApproval to true for workspace write, delete and execute_command tools, and expose a one-line agent-wide requireToolApproval default.
Make LocalSandbox auto-select bwrap/Seatbelt when available and refuse host execution without an explicit isolation: 'none' opt-out.
Ship observability with a local storage exporter on by default so every tool call and approval is recorded.
Implement the documented 30s LocalSandbox command timeout and add a default run wall-clock limit.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.

Scored the framework (@mastra/core, @mastra/mcp, @mastra/memory, server adapters, observability) at default constructor arguments; mastracode, the agent-controller harness (with its yolo mode), deployers, and the many workspace/integration packages were only sampled.
Remote sandbox providers under workspaces/ (E2B, Daytona, Modal, etc.) were not reviewed in depth; the C4 alternative scores the core bubblewrap backend.
The optional editor's stored MCP client routes are an opt-in path and were not scored as default.
No reviewer-steering text was found in AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or README.md.
